facts.text: Primm Springs grew from a mid‑1830s watering spa founded by the John Primm family, who named the springs after their own homestead.
The resort expanded in the 1860s under the Estes family, adding a dance pavilion, bowling alley, and the flagship Estes House with 21 rooms.
Primm Springs’ mineral waters—black sulphur, white sulphur, lime, calomel, and arsenic—were famed for curative properties and drew guests for health and leisure.
The Peavine Railroad, completed in 1896, brought wealthy travelers in private cars, boosting the resort’s popularity during its heyday.
After World War II, the resort closed in 1945, reopening only for meals until 1965 before floods and abandonment left many buildings in disrepair.
In 1986 the Primm Springs district was listed on the National Register of Historic Places, preserving its 1836‑1935 vernacular resort heritage.
